incidents.title: United States convicts newspaper editor Jacob Frohwerk under the Espionage Act, June 1918
incidents.summary: Jacob Frohwerk, an associate editor of the German language newspaper the Missouri Staats-Zeitung, was tried and convicted in June 1918 under the Espionage Act of 1917 for publishing articles opposing American participation in the First World War, and was sentenced to ten years in prison on each of twelve counts, to run concurrently. The Supreme Court of the United States upheld the conviction on March 10, 1919.
incidents.what_happened: Jacob Frohwerk was indicted for conspiring with Carl Gleeser to violate the Espionage Act of June 15, 1917, while the two were preparing and publishing the Missouri Staats-Zeitung, a German language newspaper based in Kansas City. Twelve articles that ran in the paper between July 6 and December 7, 1917, argued against sending American soldiers to France and criticized the military draft. A federal jury convicted Frohwerk on all but one count, and the trial court sentenced him to a fine and to ten years in prison on each remaining count, the later terms to run concurrently with the first. Frohwerk appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, arguing the prosecution violated his First Amendment right to free speech. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, writing for the Court, ruled on March 10, 1919, that criticizing the war was not automatically protected once it was joined to a conspiracy to obstruct military recruiting, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
incidents.stated_justification: Prosecutors charged that the twelve articles amounted to attempts to cause disloyalty, mutiny and refusal of duty in the military and naval forces of the United States, in violation of the Espionage Act.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The ruling meant an editor of a small circulation foreign language newspaper could be convicted and imprisoned for articles critical of the war, extending the standard the Court had set the same term in Schenck v. United States.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The United States had entered the First World War in April 1917 and introduced a national draft, and federal prosecutors brought Espionage Act cases against numerous newspapers and speakers who opposed the war effort.
incidents.outcome_note: The Supreme Court's ruling left Frohwerk's conviction and ten year sentence in place.

incidents.title: United States convicts Mother Earth editor Emma Goldman of draft conspiracy and bars her magazine from the mail
incidents.summary: Emma Goldman, editor of the anarchist magazine Mother Earth, was convicted with fellow anarchist Alexander Berkman of conspiring against the newly enacted Selective Draft Law and received the maximum two year sentence and a ten thousand dollar fine. Postal authorities then withdrew Mother Earth's second class mailing privileges, and Goldman was deported from the United States in 1919.
incidents.what_happened: Emma Goldman had edited and contributed to Mother Earth, an anarchist magazine published in New York since 1906. After Congress enacted the Selective Draft Law on May 18, 1917, requiring men to register for military conscription, Goldman and fellow anarchist Alexander Berkman were arrested in New York within weeks on charges of conspiring to induce men to refuse to register. A jury convicted both, and the trial court imposed the maximum sentence available under the conspiracy statute: two years in prison and a ten thousand dollar fine. The Supreme Court of the United States, hearing the case as Goldman v. United States, affirmed the conviction on January 14, 1918, rejecting arguments that there had been no evidence of guilt to submit to the jury. After Goldman's conviction, postal authorities denied Mother Earth its second class mailing privileges, cutting off the inexpensive postal rate the magazine needed to reach subscribers nationwide, and the magazine was suppressed. Goldman served her sentence, and in December 1919 she was deported from the United States.
incidents.stated_justification: The government charged that Goldman and Berkman conspired to induce men liable for the draft under the Selective Draft Law of May 18, 1917, to disobey the law by failing to register.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Mother Earth, the magazine Goldman edited, was suppressed after the Post Office withdrew its second class mailing privileges following her conviction.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The United States had entered the First World War in April 1917 and introduced a national draft that spring, and federal authorities moved against anarchists, socialists and other war opponents under new wartime laws.
incidents.outcome_note: Goldman's conviction stood, and she was deported from the United States in 1919.

incidents.title: Britain's Official Press Bureau controls newspaper coverage of the First World War
incidents.summary: Weeks after Britain entered the First World War, Prime Minister Herbert Asquith told the House of Commons that the Official Press Bureau was the sole channel through which the Admiralty, the War Office and other departments released naval and military information to newspapers. Members of Parliament later complained in the Commons that the Bureau delayed and withheld war news from the public.
incidents.what_happened: The First World War began for Britain on August 4, 1914, and within weeks the government set up the Official Press Bureau to control the release of naval and military information to the press. On August 27, 1914, Prime Minister Herbert Asquith told the House of Commons that the Bureau was the mouthpiece through which the Admiralty, the War Office and other public departments made war news public, and that the government had considered but decided against adding trained journalists directly to the Bureau's own staff, associating them instead with the cable censors. On November 12, 1914, member of Parliament Sir William Bull moved an amendment to the Address in reply to the King's Speech, telling the Commons that "the Press censorship started badly" and that officials had delayed and withheld accounts of events at the front for hours or days at a time. The Bureau remained the government's central channel for war news, and members of Parliament continued pressing ministers about delays in releasing information to newspapers.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said that all information that could be given without prejudice to the public interest would be given fully and promptly, but that naval and military considerations required screening war news before its release.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Newspapers depended on the Press Bureau for authorized war news, and journalists were associated with the Bureau's cable censors rather than given independent access to military information.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Britain had just entered the First World War, and the government sought to prevent newspapers from publishing information that might aid German forces or reveal the movements of British troops.
incidents.outcome_note: The Press Bureau continued controlling war news months later, when members of Parliament again raised complaints in the House of Commons on November 12, 1914.

incidents.title: Ottoman Empire bars lawmakers and officials from editing newspapers and jails a leading editor
incidents.summary: In March 1913 the Ottoman government amended its 1909 press law, barring members of parliament and state officials from serving as newspaper editors and applying the ban retroactively to every periodical already in print. The revision followed the martial court prosecution of Tanin editor Huseyin Cahid, who was jailed for continuing to publish after a protest suspension in 1912.
incidents.what_happened: The Ottoman Parliament had passed a comprehensive press law in 1909 requiring newspapers to register with the government and giving officials power to suspend and fine periodicals. Publishers exploited a loophole in the law, having suspended papers reappear under different names to escape court orders. Tanin, edited by Huseyin Cahid, suspended its own publication between July 28 and August 8, 1912, in protest of the dissolution of parliament. Shortly after Tanin resumed publishing, a martial court sentenced Cahid to one month in prison on charges that his articles threatened public order. Provincial governors, responsible for enforcing the law, complained it was too weak, and on February 16, 1913, a revision gave police power to confiscate periodicals that published obscene material. On March 9, 1913, the government extended the law further: it barred members of the Ayan and Mebusan houses of parliament and all state officials from becoming newspaper editors, and applied the ban retroactively to every periodical already in print.
incidents.stated_justification: Officials said the existing law was too weak for provincial governors to enforce, and Huseyin Cahid was prosecuted on charges that his newspaper articles threatened public order.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Lawmakers and officials who edited newspapers had to give up those positions once the March 1913 ban took retroactive effect, and editors who had evaded suspension orders by reappearing under new names lost that option.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Committee of Union and Progress had just retaken control of the Ottoman government in a coup in January 1913, after a period in which opposition newspapers had used loopholes in the 1909 press law to keep publishing despite suspension orders.
incidents.outcome_note: The March 1913 amendment and its retroactive ban on lawmakers and officials editing newspapers remained the law under the Committee of Union and Progress government.
